identity.description: Professional military, garrison or campaign service
Agricultural worker, tied to seasonal cycles and land tenure
Pastoral nomad or settled herder, often marginal to urban centers
Birth attendant, keeper of women's mysteries and infant rites
Clay worker, shapes vessels for storage, ritual, and burial
Hide worker, ritually impure profession due to contact with carcasses
Smith of copper, bronze, or iron — a liminal profession with fire mastery
Literate professional, trained in cuneiform or alphabetic script
Seafarer of the great sea, knows coastal routes and foreign ports
Hired sword, serves whoever pays — often foreign to the land
Bonded laborer, whether debt-slave, captive, or born into service
Woman without male protection, marginal but sometimes powerful
Child without parents, dependent on kin or community charity
One driven from homeland by conquest, crime, or catastrophe
Displaced by war or famine, arrived from elsewhere seeking shelter
Cultic functionary at Canaanite shrines, served Asherah or other deities
Woman who suckles another's child, often of higher status households
Arbitrator of disputes, sometimes military leader in pre-monarchic Israel
Guardian of gates, walls, or fields — sees what passes in the night
Professional keener, woman who leads funeral laments and death rites
Elite warrior who drives war chariots, requires wealth and training
Master of the ov, practitioner who consults the dead — the forbidden art
Reader of omens — entrails, flights of birds, cast lots
Senior member of community, holds authority through age and lineage
Temple officiant, authorized to perform sacrifice and maintain cult
Military officer commanding infantry or garrison
Merchant who moves goods between settlements and cultures
Young person, not yet adult, often unnamed in the record
Textile worker, often female, produces cloth and garments
Processor of olives, produces oil for lamps, food, and anointing

deathContext.description: Died in combat — sword, spear, arrow, or siege
Died of pestilence — the arrows of Resheph, the striking hand
Died of hunger when the rains failed and the grain ran out
Offered at the Tophet, passed through the fire to Molek
Killed by human hand outside of war — blood that cries from the ground
Died full of years, gathered to the ancestors in proper time
Died bringing forth life — mother or infant at the dangerous hour
Taken by water — sea, river, cistern, or flash flood
Put to death by authority — stoning, impalement, or blade
Died during the siege of a city — starvation, assault, or the final sack
Consumed by flames — accident, arson, or burning city
Death circumstances lost to time — the bone remembers what the record forgot
Left to die — infant, outcast, or wounded abandoned
Died in cultic context — foundation deposit, accompany burial, or sacred killing
Died by mischance — fall, collapse, animal, or failed work
No one present at the passing — no rites, no witnesses
Surrounded by kin at the end — proper death, proper mourning

relational.description: Bound in service to a master — king, governor, or patriarch
Received proper burial from surviving offspring — the good death
No one came, no one mourned, no one performed the rites
Broke faith with one who trusted — the weight never lifted
Trained the next generation in a craft — hands shaped hands
First ancestor of a named house — the root others branch from
Took a spouse from another people — mixed household, mixed loyalties
Outlived offspring — the grief that does not end
Last survivor of household or generation — alone among strangers
Died with obligations unfulfilled — to creditors, to gods, to kin
Gave service to the house of a god — priest, servant, or dedicated one
Performed the oil rite at a standing stone — maintained the cult place
Led soldiers in battle — responsible for lives and deaths
Stood between another and harm — bodyguard, parent, or oath-bound
Trusted and was failed — the wound of broken faith
Saw the end of the Bronze Age world — the burning cities, the refugees
Participated in the funerary feast — communion with ancestors through wine

cultural.description: Sea Peoples descendant settled in the pentapolis — Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath, Gaza
Highland dweller of the central hill country, worships Yahweh
Southern Israelite of Judah, centered on Jerusalem and Hebron
Indigenous population of the lowlands and coastal plain, pre-Israelite religion
Coastal Canaanite of Tyre, Sidon, Byblos — seafarers and traders
Subject or official of Pharaoh, from the empire that once ruled the land
Western Semitic people of the Middle Bronze Age, ancestors of many
Migrants who destroyed the Bronze Age world — arrived by ship, memory of another land
Descendant of Esau, dweller in the red hills south of the Dead Sea
Dweller east of the Dead Sea, worships Chemosh
Syrian highlander, speaks Aramaic, arrives in the Iron Age
Worships Baal Hadad, lord of storm and rain, rider of clouds
Venerates Asherah, mother goddess — keeps her figurines, anoints her pole
Worships Yahweh, the god of Israel — pre-centralization, bamah worship
Venerates Dagon, Philistine deity of grain or fish, temples at Ashdod and Gaza
Venerates Resheph, plague-god and archer, Canaanite-Egyptian syncretism
Worships El, father of the gods, creator — absorbed into Yahwism by Iron Age II
Venerates Anat, warrior goddess, sister-consort of Baal — blood and victory
Acknowledges Mot, the death-god whose domain is Sheol — not worshipped but feared
Worships multiple deities, hedges bets across traditions
Maintains the cult of household dead — feeds them, consults them, remembers
Worships at high places — hilltop shrines with masseboth and asherim
Attends the funerary banquet — wine, meat, and communion with the dead
Maintains household gods — small figurines of ancestors or deities
Possesses pillar figurine of Asherah — domestic worship despite official prohibition
Tends standing stones with oil — maintains the covenant marker
Present at the Burning Ground — witnessed or assisted the offering
Consults the dead, chirps and mutters — the forbidden art
From the central hill country — terrace farming, pastoralism, kinship networks
From the maritime settlements — Ashkelon, Gaza, Dor, Joppa, Acco
Lived in or served the temple precinct — priests, servants, dedicants
From a military settlement — Egyptian outpost or Philistine stronghold
Lived along the Way of the Sea or King's Highway — cosmopolitan, mixed
From semi-nomadic herding groups — sheep, goats, seasonal movement
Educated in temple scribal school — literate, ritualized, hierarchical
Fights in Sea Peoples or Philistine military tradition — round shield, straight sword
Born to a family of cult officiants — Levite or Canaanite temple family

disposition.description: Bound by obligation — to lord, to lineage, to oath, to role
Hot anger that outlasted death — grievance, violation, or thwarted will
Sorrow that did not end with breathing — loss carried into Sheol
Knows their worth — achievement, lineage, or skill demanded recognition
Gave self to something greater — god, master, love, or cause
Terror that followed into death — of gods, of enemies, of the unknown
Did what worked — survival, deal-making, moral flexibility
Cared for others — parent, friend, healer, or generous stranger
Tasted injustice and never forgot — cheated, overlooked, or wronged
Wanted to know — the asking spirit that did not quiet in death
Something left undone, unsaid, or wrong — the weight of what was not
Keeps still — whether by choice, trauma, or the forgetting of ages
Expects obedience — ruled in life, expects deference in death
Wants something — offerings, attention, warmth, what was denied

taboo.description: Refuses to name the Israelite god — devotee of another tradition
Cannot discuss what was given at the Tophet — the silence is absolute
Something terrible about origin — abandonment, shame, or violence
Refuses commands — was sovereign, or was enslaved and will not be again
Cannot speak the divine name they served — sacred terror or broken faith
Bound to the land — drowned, or never arrived, or the sea took everything
Anchored to place of death or burial — cannot travel with the practitioner
Someone did them wrong and the wound does not close
Part of the past is lost or suppressed — cannot or will not recall
The topic of offspring produces silence — loss, sacrifice, or shame
Refuses to admit how things ended — pride or delusion that survived death
Someone broke faith but the name is unspeakable — too painful or too dangerous

era.description: The present of the reference canon — ~1000-700 BCE. Israelite monarchy, Philistine pentapolis.
The age of the Sea Peoples and collapse — ~1200-1000 BCE. Everything changed.
The age of Ugarit and great kingdoms — ~1550-1200 BCE. Egyptian empire, Canaanite city-states.
The patriarchal age — ~2000-1550 BCE. Amorite kingdoms, Hyksos in Egypt.
The first cities and temples — ~3300-2000 BCE. Urban dawn, Canaanite foundations.
Before memory — the Rephaim, the giants, the deep past that even the dead have forgotten.
